explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Hananiah, a prophet from Gibeon, speaks up in the house of the LORD, with the priests and all the people right there. No back alley, no whispering. That's like announcing your big news in the group chat instead of sending one text.

The palace is a fair guess, since Zedekiah, king of Judah, had only just begun to reign. But the text puts this in the house of the LORD. The priests and all the people are standing there, and that's where Hananiah says it to Jeremiah, the prophet.
Gates are busy spots, I'll give you that. But this scene isn't at the gate. Hananiah speaks in the house of the LORD, with the priests and all the people there to hear it.

That's the word. Hananiah says, "I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon." Jeremiah has been wearing a yoke as a sign (Jeremiah 27:2), so a message about a broken yoke lands right in front of him. Hananiah brings it as good news.

Strengthened is the opposite of what Hananiah says. His message is that the yoke of the king of Babylon is broken. Jeremiah's earlier word was to put their necks under that yoke and live (Jeremiah 27:12), so the two prophets are pulling in different directions.
Sealed is what I do to a cookie box, friend, not what Hananiah says about a yoke. His word is that the LORD has broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Nothing in his message gets sealed.

Right on the money. Hananiah says, "Within two years I will restore to this place all the articles of the house of the LORD…" Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried them off to Babylon. Notice he puts an actual date on it, not a vague "someday."

Ten years would be a long wait for a promise, but that's not Hananiah's number. He says within two years, and he says it for the articles of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carried off. Two years is a short clock.
Seven years is a nice round number, but Hananiah doesn't use it here. He says within two years. That short timeline matters, because it makes his promise easy to check later.

True. Hananiah says the LORD will restore Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, along with all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon. Jeconiah was one of the people carried off (Jeremiah 27:20). Hananiah's promise list keeps growing: articles, a king, all the exiles.

It's actually true that Hananiah says this. He says the LORD will restore Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and all the exiles from Judah who went to Babylon. Jeconiah is one of those carried off (Jeremiah 27:20). It's a big promise, and Jeremiah is about to answer it.
True. The first thing out of Jeremiah's mouth is "Amen!" He goes on, "May the LORD do so!" I bet that surprised some folks in the crowd, since the two prophets sound like they're on opposite teams.
It's true, friend. Jeremiah starts with "Amen!" and then adds, "May the LORD do so!" He wants the articles and the exiles back from Babylon. It's after that that he says "Nevertheless."

Yes. Jeremiah says the prophet who prophesies peace will be recognized "only if the word of the prophet comes true" as the one the LORD has truly sent. That's the test. It isn't how loud the prophet is or how good the news sounds.

Speed isn't part of Jeremiah's test. He says a prophet of peace will be recognized as one the LORD has truly sent only if the word of the prophet comes true. Fast or slow, it comes down to whether it happens.

Talking first doesn't win anything here. Jeremiah says the prophet who prophesies peace is recognized as truly sent "only if the word of the prophet comes true." Being first in line gets you no credit.
That's it. Hananiah "took the yoke off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it." Snap, in front of everybody. Hananiah's message was already a broken yoke, and now he acts it out.
No, Hananiah doesn't wear it. Nothing in the text puts that yoke on his neck. He takes it off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it.

explanations.answer: He throws it in the fire
explanations.explanation: No fire in this scene, friend. The text says Hananiah took the yoke off Jeremiah's neck and broke it. I know it feels like a fire would make a bigger show, but breaking it is what the text gives us.
Yes. Hananiah says the LORD will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, "off the neck of all the nations." This isn't only about Judah anymore. He's talking big.
The priests are standing right there, but they aren't what Hananiah names. He says the LORD will break Nebuchadnezzar's yoke off the neck of all the nations. That's a lot wider than one room.

Hananiah and Jeremiah are the two prophets in the room, I'll give you that. But Hananiah's word isn't about prophets. He says the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, will come off the neck of all the nations.

Not quite. Jeremiah doesn't fire back on the spot. The text says he "went on his way," and it's shortly after that the word of the LORD comes to him (Jeremiah 28:12). He had no instant comeback, and he waited for a word.

Right, it's false. After Hananiah breaks the yoke, Jeremiah goes on his way. Only shortly after does the word of the LORD come to him. I'd have had a whole speech ready, which is why I'm glad I'm not Jeremiah.

Yes. The LORD says, "You have broken a yoke of wood, but in its place you have fashioned a yoke of iron." Wood to iron is an upgrade nobody asked for. Hananiah's yoke is gone, and what replaces it is harder.
Bronze is a decent guess, since it's another metal. But the text says iron. The LORD tells Jeremiah to say that Hananiah broke a yoke of wood and made a yoke of iron in its place.
A yoke of stone sounds heavy, but it's not what the LORD says. The word to Hananiah is that he broke a yoke of wood and fashioned a yoke of iron in its place. Iron, friend.

That's the word. Jeremiah says, "Listen, Hananiah! The LORD did not send you, but you have persuaded this people to trust in a lie." That's a serious charge. The people were trusting something, and Jeremiah says it was a lie.
The king is not what Jeremiah names here. He tells Hananiah that the LORD did not send him, and that the people have been persuaded to trust in a lie. The trust went to the wrong place.

Dream sounds like it could fit, but Jeremiah doesn't say it. He says Hananiah has persuaded this people to trust in a lie. Trust is what goes into a good recipe, and here it went into the wrong thing.

Yes. The LORD says, "You will die this year because you have preached rebellion against the LORD." And the text tells us that in the seventh month of that very year, Hananiah died. I think this is a heavy part, and it's okay to feel that.

Not next year. The word Jeremiah gives is that Hananiah will die this year. The text says it happened in the seventh month of that very year (Jeremiah 28:17). I think it's a heavy moment, so let's take it slowly.

Seven years isn't what the LORD says. The word is, "You will die this year." The seventh month of that very year is when Hananiah died, so the seven is a month and not a number of years. I think this one is a heavy part of the story.
